iterations.theme: The medical calling, an individual approach to childbirth, and the power of motherhood with Dr. Petra Podobnik

sections.subtitle: Growing up in a medical family and the power of motherhood outside the white coat
sections.screenshot_description: Dr. Petra Podobnik speaks about her most important life role as a mother in the premises of the Specijalna bolnica Podobnik.
sections.content:
Host Ana Radišić began the conversation at a special location – in the Specijalna bolnica Podobnik, a place where new lives come into the world every day. Her guest, Dr. Petra Podobnik, matured professionally and privately in that space, so she herself admitted how it is somewhat unusual for her to stay in the hospital in civilian clothes instead of a doctor's coat. Although she cares for patients and babies every day, Dr. Podobnik points out that outside of work, her role as a mother comes first.

For her, motherhood was a deeply transformative experience in which she feels the happiest. The well-being and health of her two children are her absolute priority, and in addition to that, she considers a healthy and supportive partner relationship, as well as close contacts with friends and family, to be extremely important for the development of every person.

The love for medicine imposed itself in her life quite naturally. Growing up with parents who were doctors – a neurologist mother who worked at the Vinogradska hospital and a gynecologist father who worked at Merkur – she witnessed their dedication every day. Before they opened a private hospital eighteen years ago, her parents worked in the state system for a long series of years. As a little girl, she often visited them during their 24-hour on-call shifts, so hospital corridors and operating rooms were not foreign to her, but rather a part of normal everyday life.

Although at one point she also thought about studying psychology or even veterinary medicine because she adores animals, the desire to work with people prevailed in favor of medicine. From her parents, she inherited a view of medicine as a true calling in which the patient is always in the first place, regardless of the exhaustion and great sacrifices that running such an institution requires.

sections.subtitle: An individual approach to childbirth, empathy, and the importance of healthy boundaries
sections.screenshot_description: Dr. Petra Podobnik explains the importance of an individual approach to every pregnant woman during childbirth.
sections.content:
During eighteen years of work at the maternity ward of the Specijalna bolnica Podobnik, more than seven thousand babies have come into the world. Dr. Petra Podobnik points out that after hundreds of performed deliveries, a doctor no longer counts concrete numbers, but rather focuses on being present with every woman. She recalled her days of specialization in the state system, where due to the large number of patients and the workload during on-call shifts, it was physically not possible to dedicate oneself to every pregnant woman as much as a doctor would want. Nevertheless, she was always guided by a thought that is still her guiding thread today: **"Maybe for me this is the tenth or twelfth delivery today, but for her it is the first or second in her life and she must remember it the way she would like to remember it."**

It was precisely out of the desire to provide patients with peace and complete dedication that their hospital was created. Dr. Podobnik emphasizes the importance of an individual approach, whereby she likes best to get to know the patient at least through the last few examinations before the delivery itself in order to feel how the woman breathes, what her expectations, wishes, and fears are.

In this process, the doctor often takes on the role of a kind of psychotherapist. In order to work on her personal development, Dr. Podobnik completed a five-year school of body-oriented psychotherapy. She applies the methods she learned there every day both on herself and in her work with patients, which helps her immensely in her approach to life and medicine. Still, great empathy also carries the challenge of setting healthy boundaries so that psychological exhaustion does not occur.

- **Understanding one's own responsibility:** Over the years, she has learned to be completely present and work from the purest intention, while at the same time realizing that every woman has her own story and that a doctor cannot influence all life circumstances.
- **Open communication:** In the relationship with patients, it is crucial to clearly state a professional opinion, especially when the rigid plans of pregnant women do not coincide with the actual medical course of childbirth.
- **Delegating obligations:** On the business front, she has learned to leave part of the tasks to others without feeling guilty, in order to preserve time for things that bring her joy privately.

sections.subtitle: Surrendering control: From traumatic experiences of patients to her own childbirth
sections.screenshot_description: Dr. Petra Podobnik recalls her own experience of childbirth and explains why it is important to surrender control.
sections.content:
Pregnancy and childbirth are phases of life that are extremely difficult to control. Despite all modern methods, science, and ultrasound examinations, doctors cannot completely predict or prevent everything. Because of this, Dr. Petra Podobnik points out that it is easiest to work with patients who come with trust and are ready to surrender to the guidance of experts. She finds special fulfillment in working with women who come in great fear due to previous severe traumas, such as multiple pregnancy losses, the loss of a child at a later stage, or extremely difficult previous deliveries. Providing such women with a sense of security and witnessing their happiness after a successful childbirth is the greatest privilege for her.

When asked by Ana Radišić what it was like to find herself in the shoes of a patient, considering that she knows everything about childbirth from the medical side, Dr. Podobnik answers that it was precisely this knowledge that helped her understand that nothing can be planned. She is the mother of a fifteen-year-old son and a ten-year-old daughter, and during her first childbirth, she was deeply surrendered to the process. Everything unfolded in the best possible order and so quickly that no one even had time to turn around, so it remained a wonderful memory for her.

To her pregnant women, who often go through numerous courses and create firm pictures in their heads about what childbirth must look like, she always advises to be flexible. It often happens that life wants to teach a woman to surrender control, so everything unfolds contrary to what was planned. She emphasizes that childbirth is an event that will come and pass in one day – whether vaginally or by cesarean section, the most important thing is that it is not traumatic and that the mother and baby are well, because only after that follows what is most important, and that is motherhood.

sections.subtitle: What a baby really needs in the first year and why caring for the mother is most important
sections.screenshot_description: Dr. Petra Podobnik speaks about the basic needs of a newborn and the pressure faced by young mothers.
sections.content:
Speaking about the first months of life, Dr. Petra Podobnik breaks numerous modern myths and points out that the needs of a newborn are actually very simple: **"A baby in the first year has very few needs. It has the need to be dry, to be fed, and the greatest need to be in contact."** She rejects outdated concepts and the fears of the environment that parents will "get the child used to being held" or spoil it. If a baby is in need, it simply needs to be held because in the first year the most important thing for it is to feel peace and security.

She recalled the wisdom of her grandmother who, although she did not know psychology, used to say that a child must never be left to cry. Once, the rule that "it takes a village to raise a child" applied, and babies were always held in someone's arms. Today, the Western world and the quick return of parents to work impose unnatural strategies such as quickly teaching a child to sleep alone in its room.

In addition to that, social networks and the environment impose a huge burden of expectations on young mothers. Dr. Podobnik emphasizes that in this period it is crucial to take care of the woman: **"The main care for the baby in the first year is absolutely the care for the mom."** The mother needs to be as well-rested as possible, and when she cannot take care of the child, her support team – partner and family – must step in. In the maternity ward, they strive to provide women with that first security, to sit with them when the natural drop in hormones, tears, and *baby blues* occur, and to show them that it is normal to ask for and receive such support.

sections.subtitle: Personal development through natural parenting and more humane conditions in the maternity ward
sections.screenshot_description: Dr. Petra Podobnik describes how the birth of her son prompted her to work on herself and study natural parenting.
sections.content:
When asked how she herself managed to reconcile high expectations in the roles of a mother, a doctor, and the daughter of a distinguished gynecologist who was the first in the region to open such a hospital, Dr. Podobnik honestly admits that it was very difficult. The key moment that prompted her to work on herself was the birth of her son. She wanted to be the best possible version of herself for him, but at that moment she was torn in a hundred directions between work and motherhood, without clearly arranged priorities.

Struggling with the initial challenges of motherhood, she found out about Tomislav Kuljiš and his IPD centar (Centar za prirodno roditeljstvo). His lectures on natural, physiological postulates and what every baby needs resonated deeply with her. She realized that everything is fine with every baby that cries or seeks constant contact, and that one's own internal defenses and restlessness are what a parent must work on in order to provide peace to the child.

She transfers such an approach into her daily work at the hospital as well. When Ana Radišić mentioned how many patients, including her female friends and male colleagues who are fathers, have only words of praise for the Specijalna bolnica Podobnik, the doctor pointed out that her greatest reward is when, through her work, she changes the experience for women who, due to previous traumas, did not have the strength to decide on a new pregnancy. More humane conditions of childbirth – in which the woman in labor has complete peace, the dedication of the staff, does not listen to a hundred other women in labor, and after childbirth stays alone in a room with her baby and partner – represent an ideal for Dr. Podobnik that, in a perfect world, should be available in every hospital system.

sections.subtitle: Self-love, life lessons from medicine, and peace in Gorski kotar
sections.screenshot_description: Dr. Petra Podobnik speaks about the importance of a doctor's warmth and presence in difficult moments for patients.
sections.content:
For Dr. Petra Podobnik, love is the absolute essence of everything – from love for children, partner, parents, and friends, all the way to respect and understanding for every person and their problems. Nevertheless, she singles out love for oneself as the greatest art and a lifelong task, but not from a selfish position. When a person builds that base, they stop acting out of fear and begin to live with complete trust in life, knowing that everything happens for a reason, and they pass through difficult situations more easily and learn from them.

Looking back on her education, she admits that she was always extremely eager for knowledge and that at the faculty she maybe even studied too much in order to have all A's, so today she would tell herself to relax a little more. Still, hard work during the faculty and specialization gave her invaluable experience and security. The most important thing that medicine taught her outside of textbooks is the value of human contact. Couples with difficult problems often come to her after having been previously frightened by five other doctors giving bad prognoses. After an hour of conversation with her, the patients leave calm. **"We cannot influence the outcomes, but it is a matter of how that person feels and how much you are there with them in such situations"**, explains the doctor.

In order to recharge her batteries and remain present on all life fronts, Dr. Podobnik finds peace in small things:
- **Going into nature:** She prefers to spend her free weekends in Gorski kotar, where her grandmother and grandfather are from. They have a family house there where she spent the happiest part of her childhood and where, along with walks in the forest, her heart is always in its place.
- **Family and exercise:** When she has to stay in Zagreb due to work, she relaxes through quality time with her children and dog, socializing with dear people, and workouts several times a week.

Concluding the conversation with Ana Radišić before returning to her patients and the operating room, Dr. Podobnik sent a simple yet powerful message: the most important thing is to be completely present in the moment we find ourselves in, because then everything in life somehow falls into place on its own.
